title: Making a leather passport holder
subtitle: Cut, edge, and saddle stitch a folded veg-tan leather sleeve that holds a standard passport and one or two cards
excerpt: How to make a passport holder from vegetable-tanned leather. Covers marking and cutting the panels, punching stitching holes, saddle stitching the edges, and finishing the edges with a beveller and burnisher.
sourceNotes: UK leatherwork trade practice. City and Guilds leatherwork syllabi (open access).

glossaryTerms.definition: Leather tanned using plant-based tannins rather than chrome. Veg-tan is firm, takes tool impressions and dye well, and develops a patina with use. The standard material for hand-stitched leatherwork projects. Available in 1.2 to 3 mm thickness; 1.5 mm is right for a passport holder.

The hand-stitching technique used in leatherwork. Two needles, one on each end of a single length of thread, pass through the same hole from opposite sides. Each stitch locks independently; if one thread breaks, the seam does not unravel. The stitch is stronger and longer-lasting than machine stitching on leather.

A multi-tine tool that punches a row of evenly spaced stitching holes through leather in one strike with a mallet. Tine spacings of 3 mm, 4 mm, and 5 mm are the most common. The tool keeps all holes aligned and at the same spacing.

content.text: A leather passport holder is a folded sleeve with two interior pockets: one that fits the passport body and one for cards. The work is cut two panels, mark and punch stitching holes with a
the three edges, and bevel and burnish the cut edges. The finished article fits a standard biometric passport (125 × 88 mm) with room to open without removing it.

. The outer panel: 190 × 140 mm (this folds in half to 95 × 140 mm, slightly larger than a passport). The inner pocket: 130 × 140 mm (this forms the card pocket when stitched to the outer across the bottom). Cut with the leatherwork knife against a steel rule on a cutting mat. Mark the stitch line 4 mm from the edges with a wing divider or a stitch groover.

Place the inner pocket panel on the outer panel at the bottom edge, flesh sides together. Mark the bottom edge stitch line and punch through both layers with the pricking iron. Work along the stitch line in one pass per iron width, aligning the last tine with the last hole on each consecutive strike. Punch the two side edges of the outer panel through both layers in the same way.

Cut a length of waxed thread at four times the length of the stitch run. Thread both needles, one on each end. Push one needle through the first hole, draw through to the midpoint of the thread. Pass the left needle through the second hole; then pass the right needle through the same hole from the other side, catching the left thread in the process. Pull both threads snug but not so tight they cut into the leather. Continue to the end, finish with two backstitches, and trim and burn the thread ends.

Run a size 2 edge beveller along all cut edges (grain side and flesh side) to remove the sharp corners. Wet the cut edges lightly with water and rub the leather burnisher back and forth until the fibres compress and the edge becomes hard and smooth. A few drops of beeswax or gum tragacanth worked into the edge before burnishing gives a better finish.

attrs.symptom: Stitching puckers or pulls to one side
attrs.cause: Thread tension was not equal on both needles.
attrs.fix: Pull both needles with equal force at each stitch. Work at a consistent pace; rushing leads to uneven tension.

attrs.symptom: The inner pocket sits at an angle inside the outer sleeve
attrs.cause: The inner panel was not centred precisely before punching.
attrs.fix: Pre-mark the alignment with pencil before punching. A small plastic set square against the bottom edge keeps the inner panel square.
